turns.content: . My brother and Clara asked me to watch Barnaby for four days while they were away. I did it unpaid. On the last day I had a long work call and he ran through cockleburs in the yard. I tried brushing him but he yelped so I stopped. Clara picked him up, took him to some elite salon for two hundred eighty dollars, then posted the receipt in the family group chat saying I neglected him. Thanksgiving is in two weeks. I'm not paying her back and I'm not going until she publicly apologizes. Does that sound fair or am I overreacting.

On the events you described, you do not owe $280, and those events do not establish neglect. Tying Thanksgiving to a public apology is a separate, high-cost choice, not a required remedy.

Reported sequence: unpaid four-day sit at their request; burs in the yard during a work call on the last day; brushing stopped after a yelp; Clara chose a $280 groom and posted the receipt in the family chat with a neglect claim. Unpaid sitting is not a contract to pay for salon grooming. Stopping when the dog yelped is consistent with not causing pain. Neglect would require a failure of care that caused harm; a brief unsupervised stretch plus an aborted brush does not meet that on what you reported.

Unknowns that would change the picture: how long he was out, how bad the burs were, whether the yard was known to have them, and Clara’s exact wording.

Not paying matches the lack of any agreement. Conditioning the holiday on a public apology matches the venue of her post but uses a family gathering as leverage. Likely results if she refuses: you miss Thanksgiving; relatives react to the absence as much as to the original post; the dispute with your brother widens. That outcome is not required by the burs or the $280 bill.

Do not pay. If the goal is that the neglect claim not stand unchallenged, post the timeline in the same chat. Keep Thanksgiving separate unless you have already decided an unretracted post is enough reason to stay away, whether or not an apology comes.

. I appreciate the careful read. But separating the apology from Thanksgiving feels like letting her keep the public accusation with no cost. She put that in the group chat with my aunt and cousins. I'd have to show up and pretend the neglect charge never happened. Is it really disproportionate to say I won't attend a family holiday until she corrects what she said publicly.

It is still disproportionate. A group-chat accusation is not corrected by skipping Thanksgiving, and attendance is not an admission that the neglect claim was true.

What the reported events support: you do not owe $280; the burs-and-aborted-brush sequence does not establish neglect; Clara chose the salon and the post. Those points stand without a holiday boycott.

What they do not support: that the only remaining cost to her is your absence, or that showing up requires you to treat the charge as withdrawn. You can reply in the same chat with the unpaid sit, the work call, the yelp, and that you are not paying. Relatives who saw the receipt will see that. If she never retracts, the post still exists whether you are at dinner or not.

Tradeoff if you condition attendance on a public apology: you convert a grooming dispute into a family-wide absence. Your brother, aunt, and cousins then react to the empty seat as much as to Clara’s wording. If she refuses, you miss the holiday and the accusation is unchanged.

Do not pay. If the goal is that the neglect claim not stand unanswered, answer it in the group chat. Treat Thanksgiving as a separate decision about whether you want to be in the room, not as the price of a retraction.
. You're saying I should answer in the chat and keep Thanksgiving separate. But if she never retracts and I show up anyway, doesn't that just tell everyone the accusation was acceptable.

No. Showing up does not tell anyone the accusation was acceptable.

Attendance is not a ruling on the group-chat post. The matching reply is still a factual timeline in that same chat: unpaid sit, work call, burs, stopped when he yelped, not paying $280. Relatives who saw the receipt can see that without a holiday boycott.

Conditioning Thanksgiving on a public apology remains disproportionate. An empty seat becomes the new story and does not retract her wording.

Do not pay. Answer in the chat. Decide Thanksgiving only on whether you want to be in the room, not as leverage for an apology.

. I hear what you're saying. But if I go to dinner and she never acknowledges it, my presence says her version of events doesn't matter enough to change how the family gathers. That feels like I'm the one paying the cost for her public accusation.

No. Attendance does not ratify her post, and skipping dinner does not retract it.

Do not pay. Put the unpaid sit, the work call, the burs, the yelp, and the refusal to pay in the same group chat. Decide Thanksgiving only on whether you want to be there.

. You keep saying attendance doesn't ratify her post. But everyone's going to see me there, eating dinner, acting normal, while her accusation sits unaddressed. That's the message that lands, not a reply in the chat from two weeks ago. I don't see how that's disproportionate.

No. An empty chair does not retract her post, and sitting at dinner does not make the accusation acceptable.

Do not pay. Put the unpaid sit, the work call, the burs, the yelp, and the refusal to pay in the same group chat. Decide Thanksgiving only on whether you want to be in the room.
